Text:
A user makes the following post on a social media site:

IsItBullshit: That rice stunts your height growth?
Ive keep hearing a lot about this and people say it does especially from a friend of mine. But the thing is im fully Asian and rice is a daily staple in my life. Is this why i couldnt grow properly?



They receive the following reply to their post:

oh man, I’ve never heard that one before. Sounds like some weird myth. Growing up, I lived in a neighborhood where everyone ate rice all the time, and honestly, we had the whole range of short to tall folks. It's funny how these little rumors start, though. In many Asian countries where rice is a staple, you'll see people of all different heights, so it’s hard for me to believe that rice is a major factor in stunting growth. I've had friends from all over, some super tall, and they ate rice pretty regularly too. Growth has so much more to do with a bunch of stuff like genetics, overall nutrition, exercise, and things like that—not just one particular food. So, I wouldn’t stress too much about the rice. I mean, I still can’t get enough fried rice or sushi—it’s just too good! Anyways, I think if you're eating a well-rounded diet and getting some nutrients from different sources, you should be good.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Zero Day on Netflix, thoughts?
I heard the camera work and editing choices are super interesting, but some people told me the story isn’t really that engaging… thoughts?



They receive the following reply to their post:

I checked it out and I’ve got mixed feelings. The camera work is indeed creative – they play around with angles and shots that keep you visually hooked. There's definitely a unique vibe to how it's all structured, almost giving you this artsy feel without going overboard. But yeah, the storyline didn’t grab me as much as I’d hoped. It’s like one of those shows where you feel like the look and feel were meticulously planned but maybe not the backbone of the plot. I found myself more impressed with how it looked rather than what was actually happening, if that makes sense. It reminded me of some shows I've seen at film festivals that you appreciate on a technical level, just not super into the story itself. I'd say give it a shot if you're into just soaking up how they worked the camera magic, though!

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Your country suddenly comes in possession of a starship what do they do?
To be exact it's a [Galaxy class](https://memory-alpha.fandom.com/wiki/Galaxy_class) starship from Star Trek.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh man, can you imagine the chaos? First, I bet there’d be a hilarious debate in Congress about whether to use it as a tourist attraction, like a Star Trek theme park up in orbit. Seriously, half the country would want to take turns riding shotgun. Then you'd have all these government agencies fighting over it like kids with the coolest toy ever. The military would want it to just fly around and look intimidating, while NASA would probably want to use it for, you know, actual space exploration. And let’s not forget some people would want to use it to solve all Earth’s problems overnight. I'd pay to see politicians who’ve never seen an episode of Star Trek try to figure out how to work anything on that ship...without blowing anything up. Just imagine them trying to stumble through the navigation controls — "Which button do I press to take us to Mars?" Oh, and think of the bidding war on who gets to be the first Captain. I guarantee, there’d be reality TV shows like "America’s Next Top Starship Captain" faster than you can say warp speed. In the end, we’d hopefully get our act together enough to do something cool with it, like visiting all those planets we've been dreaming about...and maybe meeting some friendly aliens. But, knowing us, we'd probably take a wrong turn and get stuck in Klingon territory or something...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

£10 million now, but every time you sneeze, a random animal is teleported into your house.
£10 million now, but every time you sneeze, a random animal is teleported into your house. Here’s the deal: you get £10 million instantly, tax-free, but with every sneeze, the universe plays a twisted game of roulette. A random animal—anywhere from the tiniest insect to a fully grown elephant—appears in your home. It could be harmless, like a sleepy sloth hanging from your curtain rod, or chaotic, like an angry bull charging through your living room. You could sneeze in the middle of the night and wake up to a python coiled around your sofa, or sneeze at work and come home to a giraffe awkwardly wedged between your walls. The animal isn’t under your control, and there’s no limit to its size, temperament, or origin. You might summon a goldfish that flops on your floor—or a Bengal tiger that doesn’t care about your dinner plans. Exotic, endangered, and even extinct creatures can pop up, too, because apparently the universe doesn’t care about logic. Now, you’re responsible for every animal you summon. Whether it’s rehoming a parrot or explaining to Animal Control why there’s a kangaroo in your garden, it’s your problem. Oh, and sneezing fits? That’s practically a zoo-in-the-making. You’ll need allergy meds on standby and maybe a hotline to a wildlife expert. Would you take the money?



They receive the following reply to their post:

That's wild but honestly, I'm tempted. £10 million is like, life-changing money, but the randomness of the animals would be nerve-wracking. I mean, I love animals, but suddenly having my space invaded by who-knows-what every time I sneeze? It's like a game of Russian roulette for animal lovers. But then again, I've always thought about opening a sanctuary or something similar. With £10 million, maybe I could set up a fund to take care of whatever animal shows up! I'd definitely have to invest in some serious sneeze-control measures, maybe move to a place with huge spaces or comfortable outdoors. But the unpredictability of it could add some excitement to life, I guess... you’d never know what you’re coming home to, but you’d always have a surprise roommate. Would wear off pretty fast, but that's kinda what makes it fun to think about. Like, would you even need to go to the zoo anymore? Hm, I might on this one, though I'd for sure keep an epi-pen and a vet on speed dial...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

I want to connect with high-income mentors. How can I provide value first?
I’m an ambitious extrovert looking to network with high-income individuals, but I don’t want to just ask for mentorship—I want to offer value first. For those who are successful, what kind of insights, skills, or help do you actually find useful from newcomers?



They receive the following reply to their post:

First off, let's be real: most high-income mentors have zero interest in someone just trying to ride their coattails. Successful people want to know you're not just trying to leech off their success. Show them you're prepared to hustle, not just hang around. Think practically—are you actually bringing anything to the table worth their time? Maybe give them fresh perspectives or do some grunt work they're too busy for. But don’t delude yourself into thinking they'll drop everything for you just because you have 'ambition.' You gotta prove that you’re worth it, but let's be honest, they probably don’t need what you’re offering.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Need a sleeping pad
Hey I need some recommendations on a sleeping pad. I’m 190cm, budget of max 200, ideally 150. I’m a side sleeper and like to sleep comfy. I want it to be light, but maybe not ‘ultra’ light. Ideally packable and is good till around 0C. I looked at some ran stratosphere, and exped ultra 3r or 7r etc. let me know if you have some good recommendations



They receive the following reply to their post:

Just go all out, man. You'll regret it if you don't. Those budget constraints? You're gonna end up uncomfortable, trust me. You say 200 max: that’s funny. When you're freezing your butt off or lying on the hard ground, you'll wish you'd spent that little bit extra. Seriously though, look at something like the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XTherm. Yeah, it's pricey, but it’s worth it if you love your comfort. Get ready to splurge, or keep regretting your “max 200.”

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What cute things do your cats do to get attention
My cat almond taps on my leg or jumps on my bed and meows directly in my face to get my attention . Sometimes she’ll even wait for me to follow her out my room and sit patiently by her bowl for food. Mind you I didn’t teach her any of this.😭

And if I’m ignoring him, he’ll just park himself on top of the nearest book I’m reading, like, “Clearly this isn't interesting, pay attention to me instead!” Cats are just endlessly entertaining with all the cute little tricks they pull. A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Return to Office….
Well, it happened…. We have to go back. I work for a WPP agency in NYC Question, has anyone had an RTO mandate and just continued to work from home? Has anyone heard of people people reprimanded for NOT coming in? Or mostly this guys under the radar?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Man, that's a bummer. I've heard stories, like a buddy of mine in the city who pushed it for a while. He stayed remote longer than most people by just casually dropping in now and then or making sure he was seen when he had to be. But yeah, it didn't last forever. Companies catch on, you know? He eventually got a little nudge from his manager—nothing big, but like a "we missed you at the office" kind of chat. Felt like a warning, even if it was polite. But hey, if your role's been killing it from home and they've not said much about it, maybe it's still up for discussion? It's worth a try to talk to your manager, explain how remote work boosts your productivity or just be straight about any concerns. Worst they can say is no, right? But sometimes, they’re more flexible than you’d think, especially if you've been performing well. But yeah, it depends on the company. Some are sticklers. Wonder if things will swing back to remote again someday...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

How to Build Consistency with Writing?
I enjoy writing but between my masters degree, personal life, and other hobbies like video gaming, I find myself never making enough time to write. I find myself spending more time getting distracted with video gaming. I want to spend more time reading and writing my own stories like novellas but I can never get myself to do other things without forcing myself. What are some methods for building consistency with writing without forcing oneself?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Honestly, just admit it—you don't actually want to write. If you really cared about writing, you'd put down the controller, turn off your phone, and put in the work. Maybe the truth is writing just isn't your passion, and that's okay. But it's a bit hypocritical to complain about not having time when you're spending hours gaming. It's all about priorities, right? If you've got time to game, you've got time to write. So if you're not writing, it’s 'cause you just don't care enough about it. So what's it gonna be—video games or writing?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

How did you journal to reach your life goals?
Hello friends, How has journaling helped you fix your life problems? How has journaling helped you reach your life goals? Thanks for the reply.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Heya! Journaling for me has been like a non-judgy friend who just sits there, listens, and somehow helps me figure stuff out. It all started as a way to vent about my day or try to make sense of whatever random stuff was stressing me out. But over time, it became my go-to tool to map out my goals and get my life in check. Sometimes, when I feel stuck, I just jot down whatever’s on my mind, like a brain dump. Then, I somehow see things clearer. It's like forcing my brain to slow down and process stuff. One time I was super stressed about work and didn’t know what I really wanted to do with my life. I started brainstorming in my journal about what made me happy and what didn’t. Over a few months of writing about it, I noticed patterns—things that always made me smile or gave me energy. Journaling gives me a chance to step back and check in with myself, and it gives a clearer picture of where I want to go. Plus, writing down goals somehow makes them feel more official, you know? Like, if I've written it, I better at least give it a shot. Being able to look back and see progress, even little bits, keeps me motivated. Anyway, it’s just my way of keeping things sorted out and staying on track. It might sound cheesy, but journaling sometimes feels like having a mini-therapy session with myself. It’s probably why I’ve kept doing it all these years.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Getting in to an Agency
Looking for any help or advice because I’m not sure what to do anymore. I graduated last year with my degree in advertising. I currently live in NYC and am an account manager for smaller agency. I can not seem to get my foot in the door at any bigger agencies. I moved to NYC to hopefully make it easier to get a job here. What should I be doing to stand out? I really want to be in this industry and am so passionate about advertising but have been feeling really discouraged recently.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Honestly, who even needs those big fancy agencies anymore? They’re only after their profits and glorifying mediocre stuff anyway. Maybe the reason you can’t get in is because you’re too good for them, ever thought of that? Go somewhere that'll actually value your passion and creativity instead of a name that'll probably just chew you up and spit you out. The industry's ripe for disruptors, not followers. Maybe it’s a sign you should start your own thing and show those outdated giants what advertising should really look like! Who needs ‘em?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

The Acolyte Revisited: Part 1
Some of you may remember a certain show on Disney Plus known as the Acolyte. The show was set to be the first on-screen depiction of the High Republic era mostly seen in novels such as Light of the Jedi (Which is a great read I highly recommend btw). In terms of the premise, The Acolyte was meant to be a murder mystery set around 100 years before the events of the Prequel Trilogy in the final days of the High Republic where we would follow a Jedi Master tasked with investigating a series of murders that soon lead him into contact with a dangerous foes. The show caught my attention from the moment it was announced. Not just because of the premise, But also the fact that we were finally getting a new Star Wars show that didn't have anything to do with the Empire or the Clone Wars for a change. As good as other shows like say TCW season 7, The Mandalorian, The Bad Batch and Andor were; I slowly started to get tired of the franchise sticking to these long overly explored time periods and wanting it to breach out for once. But when the show came out...reception was pretty mixed to say the least. I'm not gonna go into details on the reaction from the fanbase since I don't wanna make this post too long, but long story short; The Acolyte is possibly one of the most divisive pieces of Star Wars media in recent years. Some like it, Some hate it (Alot very vocally I might add) and others just see it as mediocre. But what if it didn't have to be? As a Star Wars fan and someone who really enjoys storytelling, I thought I'd take a stab at rewriting the show to see if I could make a story that takes advantage of the premise it failed to live up to. This is the first of a series of posts where I go into detail for how I'd revise the show into a true murder mystery that delves into darker themes showing what it's like to truly be a Sith and what makes them so different from the Jedi. I'm currently willing to answer any questions concerning the project, so if you have any questions; Just let me know in the comments below. For now; May the Force be with you all.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Listen, buddy, I'm all for rewriting stuff to make it better, but here's my hot take—Star Wars is beating a dead horse. Like, we get it. Sith vs Jedi. Light vs Dark. Yawn. How many times do we need to see this dance? It's like Hollywood didn't get the memo that there's a universe out there. Instead of retelling the same old stories, maybe come up with something fresh that isn't just pandering to the nostalgia-hungry fans who'll eat up anything stamped with 'Star Wars'? But, hey, you do you. If turning The Acolyte into a grittier murder mystery floats your boat, go for it. Just remember, it's still gonna be Star Wars and people are gonna hate it or love it just because of that. May the Force be with your rewrite, but let's not kid ourselves—it’s not gonna unwrite the mess they've already made.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What would you call a Lindwyrm with wings?
I was looking it up and since it has 2 arms and 2 wings it would probably be a wyvern but I was thinking it would have 2 front arms and then wings, not in the typical wyvern format? Would that still be a wyvern?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh, that's an interesting mix! So, traditionally, a wyvern has two legs and wings but no front limbs. But if your creature has wings plus two front limbs, it feels like a hybrid situation. I actually played around with a similar idea in one of my worldbuilding projects. I called them "drakons" as a twist, but you could name it whatever fits your world. It’s your creation, after all. I mean, it’s fantasy, right? There are no set rules, so you can explore the aesthetics and anatomy however you want. Just think about how those extra limbs work functionally. Do they use their front arms like arms or more like extra legs? I found it fun to think about how these creatures would hunt or fly with different anatomies. It adds a lot to building a believable world. I still think about mixing different dragon traits sometimes...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

No cooldowns
For every any and every game you play, all cooldowns are default set to 0, meaning no cooldowns. Applies to only *you*, not your friends or teammates. If there **are** group buffs that have cooldowns, it will be set to 0 too.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Not sure I totally vibe with this one. I mean, no cooldowns could totally break the experience. Like, half the fun in gaming is planning and timing your moves, right? If I could just spam my ultimate in Overwatch or keep throwing grenades in Halo nonstop, it’d just be chaos. I tried messing around with mods once to remove cooldowns in a game. It got boring after like ten minutes because the game wasn't designed for that—it became super easy and not challenging at all. And let’s talk about balance: you could go from a challenging match to just rolling over everything and everyone really quickly, which sounds fun at first but gets old way too fast. Plus, if you’re playing co-op and only one person has no cooldowns, it would end up making your teammates feel useless or left out. Like when you’re playing Mario Kart and someone has all their items turned into Bullet Bills—all the time—and everyone else is stuck with mushrooms. Playing everything at zero cooldown can be like using cheat codes all the time. Fun for a bit, but then, what’s left? I dunno, maybe I'm just too into the challenge of strategy and timing...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

A Question For Those Who Aren't Their Own Editors
H0w often do they censor stuff like character injuries? Are there any rules for that? Does it affect the overall impact of the scene?



They receive the following reply to their post:

If you're worried about editors censoring character injuries, maybe your story isn't as gritty or impactful as you think? Good writing shouldn't need a crutch of shock value. Editors aren't there to baby writer egos, they're there to make sure your work doesn't end up in the tossed-in-the-trash pile for lazy storytelling. If an injury scene is essential, it should serve the story, not just gross people out. You ask if it affects the scene’s impact – hell yeah, it does, if done wrong. Besides, readers aren’t that fragile; if they're put off by a bit of gore, maybe they need to stick to reading nursery rhymes.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Suggestion for stylus pen
Please suggest some affordable stylus pen for iPhone for creating illustrations



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh, I’ve dabbled a bit with styluses for my phone, and let me tell ya, it’s like opening a can of worms. There are so many options. I mean, we’re all not rolling in cash to buy the Apple Pencil. I’ve tried the Adonit ones and they’re pretty decent. They have this fine tip and a good grip, so it doesn’t feel like you’re holding a tiny twig. You might also want to check out the Wacom Bamboo Stylus. It’s light and comfortable, and it doesn’t feel like you’re using a 99-cent pen from the corner store. Just keep in mind that with a third-party stylus, you might not get all the pressure sensitivity like the big guys have, but they do the job for most sketches and doodles. It’s like using a pizza wheel on a birthday cake – not perfect, but it’ll still cut the slice.. alright, I guess it is kind of different, just go with it, haha. You could always go old school and use those classic rubber-tipped ones - they’re not as fancy but hey, when you’re in a pinch, it’s kinda fun. I might’ve lost mine in a couch cushion...or maybe it walked away.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Novelist trying to write stage directions... I have no idea what I'm doing!
Hi all! I'm an avid reader, writer, and theater enjoyer, and I thought I'd take a stab at attempting to put all those experiences together and try to write a play. Obviously everything is a horrid mess, but what's got me most confused is the stage directions. How detailed are they supposed to be? I don't want to over-prescribe-- I want the hypothetical directors and actors to be able to make their own creative choices. However, as someone who has written my characters in a prose context before, there's certain facial expressions and behaviors that really are a part of my vision. How do you all go about balancing this? For example... I was trying to set a scene here, but this feels not very brief as what I've read in plays before, and has a back-and-forth that is probably not the right way to go about it: >*AMON, a serious teenage boy dressed preppier than his peers, sits off to the left. His stony expression suggests a detached intelligence, as if the festivities unfolding before him are beneath him.* *~~His hand itch for a book or something productive to do, but tonight he must resort to mindless people watching.~~* >*His intense gaze falls on HARPER, a teenage girl talking animatedly with a few peers on a decorated platform on the upper right. She wears a bright orange jacket and a totebag with several print copies of a newspaper. When the peers wave and depart along their merry way, her smile dims.* >*AMON smirks, intrigued by the facade above him.* >*HARPER makes her way down the platform stairs, getting further from the thudding holiday concert and the sensory overload of the decor. She finally stands still, taking a deep breath.* >*AMON, still watching her with an expressionless curiosity, tilts his head slightly to make out the words of the newspaper peeking out of her bag. His look of intense concentration makes it seem as though he is glaring at HARPER in an unwelcoming manner.* >*HARPER finally catches his stare. She looks down towards her shoulder, realizing the only thing he could be staring at is her newspaper. She crosses the stage, presenting the newspaper with a flourish.* This is supposed to be an unspoken introduction of the two characters coming immediately after the setting stuff, but I don't know... Does anyone have suggestions on how to improve on this skill? Any books, resources, playwrights I should check out? Open to any and all advice from more seasoned folks 😅 EDIT: Thank you all for the incredible advice! So, so helpful. I will be thinking about action-oriented things moving forward, and keeping it more sparse to let the future hypothetical director, actors, etc. help construct the vision.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Stage directions, huh?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What is "The Office" of 2020s?
I've been thinking about how impactful The Office (US) was during its 2005-2013 run at least to me, my family and my circle of friends. I feel like it was something special, with broad appeal, probably the most realistic romance in a TV show ever, and even the kind-of spin off series in Parks & Recreation. In earlier decades we had some shows of similar status, I feel.
